title: Squat depth and knee flexion
text: During a rehabilitation squat, knee flexion is typically progressed within a pain-free range. A commonly cited target for functional strength is a knee angle of about 90 degrees (parallel thigh), but earlier rehabilitation phases often stay closer to 100 to 120 degrees of knee flexion until the joint tolerates a deeper range. Depth should be individualised to the patient's range of motion and the surgical or injury protocol.

title: Knee alignment over the ankle
text: Excessive forward translation of the knee past the toe during a squat increases patellofemoral joint compressive force. Keeping the shin roughly vertical and driving the hips backward reduces anterior knee stress. For patellofemoral pain rehabilitation, coaches often cue the patient to sit back and keep the knee stacked over the ankle.

title: Torso lean during a bodyweight squat
text: A moderate forward torso lean is normal during a squat, but excessive forward flexion (typically more than about 45 degrees from vertical) increases lumbar spine load and shifts effort away from the quadriceps. Cueing the patient to engage the core, keep the chest up, and hinge at the hips helps maintain a neutral spine.

title: Eccentric and concentric tempo
text: Slowing down the eccentric (lowering) phase of a squat to about 3 seconds while keeping the concentric (rising) phase at 1 to 2 seconds increases time under tension and can support tendon rehabilitation. Very fast reps limit the ability to control form and are usually reserved for late-stage return-to-sport protocols.
